title: My Journey So Far
summary: Stories from a small town to engineering college — the moments that shaped who I am.

chapters.title: Childhood
chapters.description: Where everything began — dusty lanes, summer games and a big joint family.

stories.title: The Day I Learned to Ride a Bicycle
stories.content:
I was eight when my uncle brought home an old, rusting bicycle. It was almost my height, and I could barely reach the pedals while sitting on the seat. For two whole weeks I fell every single evening — scraped knees, bruised elbows, and one memorable crash into the neighbourhood water tank.

My father would hold the back of the seat and run behind me down the lane. One evening he quietly let go, and I didn't notice. I rode alone for almost fifty metres before I realised no one was holding me. When I turned around, he was standing far back, laughing and waving.

That was the first time I understood something I still believe: most of the time, the support we depend on has already taught us enough to stand on our own. The bicycle is long gone, but that fifty-metre ride is still the proudest distance I have ever covered.

stories.title: Childhood Friends and the Mango Tree
stories.content:
Behind my grandmother's house there was an old mango tree that belonged to nobody and everybody. Every summer vacation, the whole neighbourhood's children would gather under it with sticks, stones and unlimited ambition.

We never actually got many mangoes — the tree was too tall and we were too small. But the trying was the point. Rafi would climb higher than anyone and throw down half-ripe mangoes that made our faces pucker for hours. Mina brought salt in a folded newspaper. We would sit in a circle under the tree, wincing and laughing at the same time.

When I visit home now, the tree is still there, much bigger. The children under it are different children. But for a second, every time I see it, I can taste that sharp, salty, half-ripe sweetness of those summers.

chapters.title: School Life
chapters.description: Classrooms, competitions, and the teachers who saw something in me before I did.

stories.title: My First Stage Speech — and How It Almost Ended in Disaster
stories.content:
In class seven, my teacher entered my name for the annual day speech without telling me. I found out two days before the event. I had never spoken on a stage in my life, and my English was far better on paper than out loud.

I practised in front of the bathroom mirror until my mother threatened to charge me rent. On the day, I walked up to the microphone, looked at four hundred students, and my mind went completely blank. Total silence for what felt like a year.

Then, from the third row, my friend Imran shouted the first line of my speech. The whole hall laughed — and somehow that laughter broke the fear. I picked up from where he shouted, and finished the entire speech without looking at the paper once. I didn't win the competition. But I won something better: proof that freezing on stage is survivable. I have spoken on many stages since, and before every single one, I remember Imran shouting that first line.

stories.title: The Teacher Who Changed My Trajectory
stories.content:
Mr. Dutta taught mathematics, but his real subject was possibility. He was the first person who told me, plainly, that a boy from a government school in a small district town could study at an IIT or an NIT — not as motivation-speaker talk, but as a plan with steps.

He lent me his own books. He stayed back after school twice a week, unpaid, to solve problems with a handful of us. When I got my NIT seat, he was the first person my father called.

The lesson he left me with is simple: never underestimate the compound interest of one adult who believes in a child early enough. These days, whenever a junior asks me anything about careers or studies, I remember that staying back after school was never optional for me — it's just rent on a debt I can never fully repay.

chapters.title: College Life
chapters.description: NIT Silchar — hostels, hackathons, and learning how big the world really is.

stories.title: The First Day That Felt Like a Movie
stories.content:
I arrived at NIT Silchar after two days of trains and buses, with two suitcases and a head full of questions. The campus gate, the red academic building, seniors on bicycles shouting directions — it was overwhelming in the best possible way.

My hostel room had three other boys from three different states. By midnight we were arguing about whose biryani was superior, and by the end of the week we were inseparable. That first night, lying in a strange bed in a strange state, I felt a kind of freedom and terror that I had never felt before.

The funniest part is how quickly 'terrifying new place' became 'the place I now miss the most'. Four years later, that room — with its broken fan and endless late-night conversations — is still the single place I would revisit if I could.

stories.title: How We Won Our First Hackathon
stories.content:
In second year, four of us entered the campus hackathon with a half-baked idea: an app to help local farmers check fair market prices. We had one laptop that overheated, one teammate who vanished to sleep for three hours, and a demo that worked exactly twice out of ten tries.

The night before the final presentation, our backend crashed completely. We rebuilt the critical parts on a friend's machine until 5 AM. At 9 AM we presented, honestly, including what was broken. The judges later told us that honesty was why we won — every other team oversold a flawless product.

Standing on that stage with the certificate, I learned the most practical lesson of my college life: people don't expect perfect. They expect honest, working, and genuinely meant to help. We won two more hackathons after that, but the first one — built on an overheating laptop and four cups of chai — will always be the sweetest.

chapters.title: Career
chapters.description: First internships, first salary, and finding work that actually matters to me.

stories.title: My First Salary and My Mother's Reaction
stories.content:
My first internship stipend was small — enough to feel real, not enough to feel rich. I bought my mother a shawl with the first part of it. Nothing expensive, just a simple warm shawl from the local market.

She held it, folded it, unfolded it again, and then went to the kitchen without saying much. Later my sister told me she had shown it to three neighbours that evening, telling each of them her son earned it himself.

I have earned more since then, but no amount has ever felt the way that first small amount felt. There is a particular kind of joy in the first proof that you can take care of the people who spent their lives taking care of you. Everything I have chased in my career since, quietly, chases that same feeling.

stories.title: The Rejection That Redirected Me
stories.content:
In my final year, I was rejected by seven companies in a row. Seven. Each rejection email arrived with the same polite, hollow language, and each one landed a little harder than the last. I started avoiding the placement cell entirely.

The eighth application was to a startup nobody on campus was talking about. I built a small working prototype for their actual product instead of just sending a resume. They hired me within two weeks.

Looking back, those seven rejections were doing something I couldn't see at the time: they were filtering out the paths that didn't fit me. The lesson I keep from that season is this — rejection is rarely a verdict on your worth. Most of the time it is just a mismatch of needs, timing, or imagination. Keep building, keep applying, and let the no's redirect you rather than define you.

stories.title: Advice I Would Give My Younger Self
stories.content:
If I could sit across from my sixteen-year-old self, I would tell him four things.

First: marks open doors, but curiosity keeps them open. Study, but never mistake the syllabus for the world. Second: start building things early and badly. The fifteen bad projects teach you more than one perfect plan. Third: choose friends who talk about ideas and hopes, not only about people. Your circle quietly sets your ceiling. And fourth: call your parents more often. The window of life where they are fully yours is smaller than it looks from eighteen.

None of these came from a book. Each one cost me something to learn — which is probably why they are the only lessons I trust enough to pass on.
